nameStory: The fin whale gets its name from the prominent dorsal fin on its back, which stands out like a ship's sail as it surfaces. Unlike some whales that barely show their fins, this massive marine mammal displays its distinctive triangular fin clearly above the waterline. Early whalers called them 'finbacks' because that fin was often the first and most obvious feature they'd spot from their boats.
description: The fin whale is an ocean giant and the second-largest whale species in the world, reaching lengths of up to 85-89 feet. These sleek marine mammals have long, slender bodies with brownish-gray coloring on top and pale undersides. They're part of the rorqual family, which means they have pleated throat grooves that expand like an accordion when feeding. Despite their massive size, fin whales are surprisingly fast swimmers and can often be seen traveling in small groups of 6-10 individuals.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Enormous whale with a long, streamlined body that can reach 85+ feet in length. The head is V-shaped when viewed from above, and the body tapers to a relatively narrow tail section, giving it a torpedo-like appearance in the water.

idTips.label: Distinctive Fin
idTips.description: Large, triangular dorsal fin positioned about two-thirds back on the body, curving backward like a shark's fin. This prominent fin is often the first feature visible as the whale surfaces and is what gives the species its common name.

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Dark brownish-gray on the back and sides with a pale white or cream-colored belly. This countershading makes them less visible to prey below and predators above when viewed from different angles.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often travels in small pods of 6-10 individuals and surfaces predictably to breathe, showing the dorsal fin and back in a rolling motion. When diving, they rarely show their tail flukes above water, unlike humpback whales.

idTips.label: Breathing Pattern
idTips.description: Creates a tall, narrow blow (water spout) that can reach 20 feet high when exhaling at the surface. The blow appears as a thin column rather than a wide spray, and they typically take 3-5 breaths before diving.

idTips.label: Speed
idTips.description: Capable of swimming at impressive speeds, often moving faster than other large whales. When traveling, they maintain a steady pace and cover great distances, earning them the nickname 'greyhounds of the sea.'

habitat: Fin whales are found in the deeper waters of the North Atlantic Ocean off New England's coast, particularly in areas where the continental shelf drops off into deeper waters. They prefer the cooler, nutrient-rich waters where their prey of small schooling fish, squid, and krill are abundant. You're most likely to spot them during whale watching trips that venture into waters at least 100 feet deep, often 10-20 miles offshore from places like Cape Cod, Stellwagen Bank, or the waters off Maine.

seasonality.spring: Fin whales begin arriving in New England waters as the ocean warms and prey becomes more abundant. This is an excellent time for whale watching as they're actively feeding and may be seen more frequently near the surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for fin whale sightings in New England waters. They're actively feeding on abundant schools of fish and krill, making them more predictable to observe during whale watching expeditions.
seasonality.fall: Still present in good numbers but may begin moving toward warmer waters for winter breeding. Their feeding behavior intensifies as they build up fat reserves for their migration south.
seasonality.winter: Most fin whales have migrated to warmer, lower-latitude waters for mating season. Sightings in New England waters become very rare during the coldest months.

funFact: Fin whales are among the loudest animals on Earth, producing low-frequency calls as low as 16 hertz that can travel hundreds of miles underwater - these sounds are so deep they're below the range of human hearing and may be how they communicate with other fin whales across entire ocean basins.
confusionNotes: Fin whales are most easily confused with sei whales, which are smaller and have a more curved dorsal fin. Remember: fin whales have a more triangular, prominent dorsal fin and are significantly larger, while sei whales have a smaller, more hook-shaped fin. Blue whales are larger but have much smaller dorsal fins and mottled blue-gray coloring.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'rorqual' comes from Norwegian and means 'furrow whale,' referring to the pleated throat grooves that all members of this whale family possess. These grooves allow their throats to expand enormously when feeding, like a pelican's pouch. Despite their massive size, fin whales were historically called 'greyhounds of the sea' by whalers because they were too fast to catch until explosive harpoons were invented.
compareHints: Compared to their close relative the common minke whale, fin whales are dramatically larger (minkes max out around 30 feet versus fin whales' 85+ feet) and have much more prominent dorsal fins. Sei whales are closer in size but have distinctly curved, hook-shaped dorsal fins and tend to surface more erratically, while fin whales have triangular fins and more predictable surfacing patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to their larger rorqual relatives in New England waters, minke whales are much smaller and more agile than fin whales, which can reach 70 feet and have asymmetrical jaw coloring.
Compared to their close relatives, sei whales are smaller than fin whales but larger than minke whales.
